passage:
Supervisor's note, research lab, end of term. Written by Farhan.
Hansa has spent eight months building a survey tool for her project on rural schools. This week the state changed its data rules, and the tool can no longer be used as planned. I expected her to push on and patch it; many students would, after eight months. Instead she came to my office with a single page. At the top: "If I were starting today, would I build this?" Her answer: no. Below it she listed what she had learned: sampling, field logistics, code she could reuse. She admitted she had felt sad and a little foolish for a day. Then she proposed a smaller interview study. I approved it, and asked Naveen to help her reuse the code.

qa.q: What did the state change this week?
qa.a: The state changed its data rules.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel about stopping the survey tool?
qa.a: She felt sad and a little foolish for a day, but didn't let that feeling push her into patching a project she wouldn't start today.

qa.q: What is useful about Hansa's single page?
qa.a: It asks whether she would start the project today, answers honestly, and lists what the eight months taught her, so the loss becomes learning instead of shame.

qa.q: How does Farhan see Hansa's choice?
qa.a: Farhan expected her to push on like many students, so the clear, calm decision seems to earn respect and a quick approval.

grounding: Shows a young woman asking whether she would start her project today, grieving the lost months briefly, and moving on without shame.

passage:
Tuesday night
Today I finally asked myself the question Ojas keeps asking: if I were starting fresh today, would I sign up for a third CA attempt? The honest answer was no. Not because I'm lazy. Because I've learned I love the analytics work at my job more than any exam hall. That hurts to write. Two years, the coaching fees, all those 5 am alarms. I cried in the bathroom for a bit, and that's okay. I'm writing down what those years gave me: accounting basics, discipline, and friends from my batch. They weren't wasted. They just aren't a reason to keep going. Tomorrow I'll tell Mummy, as her daughter, not as a failed student, and I won't apologise.
Trisha

qa.q: What does Trisha say she loves more than any exam hall?
qa.a: Trisha loves the analytics work at her job more than any exam hall.

qa.q: Why did Trisha cry in the bathroom?
qa.a: Letting go of two years, the fees and the early alarms felt like a real loss, and she let herself grieve it before moving on.

qa.q: What steps did Trisha take that others could copy?
qa.a: Ask whether you'd start the plan today, let yourself feel the loss, write down what the effort taught you, and then share the decision without apologising.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel on hearing Trisha's answer?
qa.a: Ojas may feel relieved and proud, since the question Ojas kept asking finally helped Trisha decide calmly.

grounding: Shows a young woman asking if she would start the exam path today, grieving its cost, noting what she learned and moving on without shame.

passage: Behind her house in a village near Dharwad, Malti had spent two years and most of her savings on a mushroom shed. Her brother Hrithik had helped build it, and her friend Pankaj from the agriculture office had brought the spawn. But every summer the humidity went wrong and the crop rotted. This July, standing in the stink of another failed batch, Malti asked herself a question Pankaj had once asked her: "If you had never built this shed, would you start it today, knowing what you know?" She sat on an upturned bucket for a long time. The answer was no. She cried a little, for the money, the early mornings, the hope. Then she wrote down what she'd learned: check water, check buyers first, start small. The next week she and Hrithik turned the shed into a shelter for her goats. "Not a waste," Hrithik said. "It's a good roof."

qa.q: How long had Malti spent on the mushroom shed?
qa.a: Two years and most of her savings.

qa.q: Why did Malti cry after deciding to stop?
qa.a: She was grieving the money, the early mornings and the hope she had put in. Stopping was right, but the loss still hurt.

qa.q: What question helped Malti decide, and what did she do after answering it?
qa.a: Whether she would start the shed today, knowing what she knows now. When the answer was no, she wrote down her lessons and turned the shed into a goat shelter.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see the end of the mushroom project?
qa.a: He seems to see it without shame, calling the shed "a good roof," which helps Malti feel the effort wasn't wasted.

grounding: A young woman in a village asks if she would start her failing mushroom shed today, grieves the cost, learns from it and moves on.

passage: In Accra, Rania had spent two years and almost all her savings turning an old van into a food truck. The city had refused her licence twice because the van was too old for the new rules. Her friend Kwame found her sitting on the van's step, the permit letter in her lap. "Appeal again?" he asked. "I was going to," she said. "I've put so much into it. I can't just stop." Then she paused. "Kwame, if I'd never bought this van, would I buy it today?" "Knowing what you know now?" "No," she admitted. "Never." She was quiet for a while, and her eyes filled. "Two years." "Two years you learned to cook for crowds and run a business," Kwame said. The next month she sold the van for parts and rented a small stall in the market. She pinned the old permit letter above the counter.

qa.q: How many times had the city refused Rania's licence?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why was Rania about to appeal again?
qa.a: Rania was afraid of losing two years and almost all her savings, so stopping felt like losing everything. Continuing seemed to protect what she had spent.

qa.q: What question changed Rania's decision, and how did she move forward?
qa.a: She asked whether she would buy the van today, knowing what she knows now. When the answer was no, she sold it for parts and rented a market stall, taking what she had learned.

qa.q: What might Kwame be feeling as Rania's eyes fill with tears?
qa.a: Kwame is likely sad for Rania but also hopeful, wanting the two years seen as learning, not failure.

grounding: A young woman abroad asks if she would buy her food-truck van today, grieves the loss, and moves on to a market stall.

passage: At 9 p.m. the lab at the institute was empty except for Urmila and the hum of the freezer. Two years on the same enzyme project, and the fourth trial had failed exactly like the first three. Her supervisor, Sarika, had left a sticky note: "Decide by Monday: continue, or switch to the soil project?" Urmila sat with her notebook and wrote a single question: If I were starting today, knowing what I know now, would I choose this? She answered honestly: No. She let herself sit with that for a while, eyes stinging. Two years. Then she made a list: what the failures had taught her, which methods she could carry to the soil work. On Monday she told Sarika, "I'm switching. I'll write up what didn't work, so nobody else loses two years." Sarika nodded. "That's a real result too."

qa.q: What did Sarika's sticky note ask?
qa.a: Decide by Monday: continue, or switch to the soil project?

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when she answered No?
qa.a: She felt sad and grieved the two years, eyes stinging, but she let herself feel it instead of hiding from it.

qa.q: How does Urmila turn the lost time into something useful?

passage:
Dear Chaitanya,
I've decided to close the weekend bakery stall. Eighteen months, every Saturday at 4 a.m., and I'm tired in a way sleep doesn't fix. For weeks I thought I couldn't stop, because of the oven I bought and all those Saturdays. Then I asked myself something you once asked me: "If you were starting today, knowing all this, would you?" The honest answer was no. I'd bake for friends, not for a stall.
I cried about it on Sunday. I'm allowed to. It was a real thing I built. But I also learned how to price, how to talk to strangers and how to get up at four without complaining, and I'm keeping all of that.
I'm not ashamed. It did its job. Now I want my Saturdays back.
Come for cake; the oven stays.
Trisha

qa.q: How long did Trisha run the weekend bakery stall?
qa.a: Eighteen months, every Saturday at 4 a.m.

qa.q: How does Trisha feel about closing the stall?
qa.a: Trisha feels sad enough to cry on Sunday, but not ashamed; proud of what was built and relieved at getting Saturdays back.

qa.q: What question helped Trisha decide, and why does it work?
qa.a: "If you were starting today, knowing all this, would you?" It looks forward instead of at the oven and the Saturdays already spent.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Chaitanya may feel touched that an old question helped, and glad to be invited for cake.

grounding: A young worker writes about asking whether they would start the stall today, grieving it and moving on without shame.

passage: Lalit, people expect me to say shutting down the app was the worst day of my life. It wasn't. The worst days were the six months before, when I kept going because of the three years already in it. Every morning I'd open the numbers, see them flat, and think, Avni, you can't quit now, look what you've spent. Then my co-founder asked me one question over chai: "If we had a blank page today, knowing what we know, would we build this?" I said no before I could stop myself. We both went quiet. I grieved it properly: I cried in the car, I sat with the team, I thanked them. Then we wrote down every lesson, and I took them to my next job. No shame in that. Only the six months I wish I'd had back.

qa.q: What did Avni's co-founder ask over chai?
qa.a: If we had a blank page today, knowing what we know, would we build this?

qa.q: What was Avni feeling in the six months before shutting down?
qa.a: Avni felt stuck and weighed down, opening flat numbers every morning but unable to quit because of the three years already spent.

qa.q: How did Avni close the chapter well?

passage: I've known Urmila since school, and last month I watched her make the hardest decision I've seen. She had spent two years and most of her savings building a small pottery studio in Bengaluru. It wasn't working. Some weeks nobody came. One evening, over tea, she asked herself out loud, "If I were starting today, knowing what I know, would I open this studio?" She was quiet a long time. Then she said, "No." I thought she'd cry. She did, a little. She said, "I'm sad about the money and the years. But I learned how to run a business, and what customers want." A week later she closed the studio and took a job teaching pottery at a design school. I haven't seen her this light in years. I'm Deepika, and I keep her question on a sticky note now.

qa.q: What did Urmila ask herself over tea?
qa.a: "If I were starting today, knowing what I know, would I open this studio?"

qa.q: How does Deepika seem to feel watching Urmila's decision?
qa.a: Deepika seems moved and admiring, surprised by Urmila's courage and inspired enough to keep her question on a sticky note.

qa.q: What made Urmila's decision wise?
qa.a: She judged from here forward, grieved the cost honestly, took the lessons, and moved on without shame.

qa.q: How did Urmila seem to feel after closing the studio?
qa.a: Urmila seemed lighter and relieved, though still sad about the lost money and years.

passage:
A Saturday in January. Afreen had spent eight months writing a novel in the evenings after work. Sitting in her Mumbai flat, she read the draft and felt it was dead. She told her friend Nandini, "I can't stop. Eight months!"

A Wednesday two weeks later. Nandini asked, "If you'd never started this novel, would you start it today?" Afreen thought hard. "No. I'd write the short stories I keep thinking about instead." She sat with that. Her eyes filled. "Eight months," she whispered. "That's okay," Nandini said. "You can be sad about it."

A Sunday in March. Afreen had written two short stories. She'd kept three characters from the novel and a lot of what she'd learned about dialogue. She printed the first story and read it aloud to Nandini, smiling. "The novel wasn't wasted," she said. "It taught me."

qa.q: How long had Afreen spent writing the novel?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: How did Afreen feel when she answered Nandini's question?
qa.a: She felt sad, her eyes filling, grieving the eight months, but also clear about what she really wanted.

qa.q: What did Afreen do that made moving on easier?
qa.a: She allowed herself to grieve, kept the lessons and characters from the novel, and started the short stories she actually wanted to write.

qa.q: How does Nandini support Afreen?
qa.a: Nandini asks a clear question and lets Afreen be sad without judging, then celebrates the new stories with her.

grounding: It shows a wise person who asks whether she would start her novel today, grieves the cost, learns from it and moves on, over several weeks.

passage: Uma, you're wondering whether to leave your MBA prep? Let me tell you what I did at twenty-five. I'd spent a year and a lot of money setting up a small tiffin service in Pune with a partner. It was losing money every month. I kept telling myself, just a few more months, or everything is wasted. My mother asked me one evening, "Nikita, beti, if you were starting today, would you open this?" I didn't answer that night. The next morning I wrote it down: No. I cried properly then, for the money and the year. I let myself feel ashamed for one day, and then I stopped. I wrote down what I'd learned: cooking at scale, handling customers, keeping accounts. Then I closed it and joined a food company. I use those lessons every day. That's what Nikita learned: look forward, not back.

qa.q: What did Nikita set up in Pune?
qa.a: A small tiffin service with a partner.

qa.q: How did young Nikita feel once she admitted the answer was no?
qa.a: Nikita cried and felt grief and a day of shame, but then felt clear enough to write down lessons and move on.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Nikita decide?
qa.a: Her mother's question about starting today helped her judge from here forward instead of by the money already spent.

qa.q: How might Nikita's mother have felt asking that question?
qa.a: Her mother probably felt caring and worried, hoping to free her daughter from the stress.

passage:
Neelam's boutique lease was up for renewal on Friday, and she had four days to decide. Her business partner Gopika had already left for a job in Delhi.

For a year, Neelam had poured everything into the little shop in Jaipur: her savings, her evenings, a loan from her uncle. Sales had never picked up.

Every time she thought of closing, she thought, but I've already spent so much.

On Tuesday night, she sat alone among the racks and asked herself one question: if I were starting today, knowing everything I know now, would I open this shop?

The answer came fast. No.

She cried then. For the money, the year, the dream. She let herself grieve it properly.

On Wednesday, she wrote down three things she'd learned: pick a busier street, test demand first, don't rush a partnership.

On Thursday, she called the landlord. She didn't renew. She felt sad, but not ashamed.

qa.q: When was Neelam's boutique lease up for renewal?
qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling after answering her question on Tuesday night?
qa.a: Neelam felt grief for the money, the year and the dream, and let herself cry for it properly.

qa.q: What did Neelam do after deciding, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Neelam grieved, then wrote down three lessons and called the landlord, so she moved forward without shame and with something learned.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel hearing that Neelam closed the shop?
qa.a: Gopika might feel sad for Neelam and perhaps relieved that she didn't keep struggling alone.

grounding: Under a lease deadline, a young woman asks if she would start her shop today, grieves the cost, learns and moves on.

passage:
Vandana had spent two years preparing for the state civil services exam. Two attempts. Countless evenings in the Nagpur library. Her friend Harsha had watched her grow thinner and quieter.

After the second result, Vandana sat in Harsha's kitchen. "Everyone says try once more. I've already put in so much."

Harsha asked, "If you were starting today, knowing what you know now, would you choose this exam?"

Vandana was quiet for a long time. She thought about the job offer from the NGO she'd been volunteering with, the work she actually loved.

"No," she said. "I wouldn't."

She cried then, for the two years and the plans she'd made. Harsha didn't rush her.

Later, she said, "I learned how to study, how to write, how to keep going. That's not nothing."

The next week, she accepted the NGO offer. She didn't feel ashamed. She felt like she'd finally chosen.

qa.q: How many attempts had Vandana made at the exam?
qa.a: Two attempts.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling after answering Harsha's question?
qa.a: Vandana felt grief for the two years and plans, and cried, but also clearer about what she really wanted.

qa.q: What made Harsha's question helpful?
qa.a: It asked Vandana to decide from today rather than from what was already spent, which made the answer clear.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt watching Vandana cry?
qa.a: Harsha probably felt tender and patient, choosing not to rush Vandana's grief.

grounding: A young woman asks whether she would start her exam preparation today, grieves the lost years and moves on without shame.

passage:
"Jyoti, you've been learning Japanese for a year and a half. Why stop now?"

"Because I asked myself something, Aditi. If I were starting today, would I pick Japanese?"

"And?"

"No. The job I wanted in Tokyo isn't what I want anymore. I love my work here."

"But all those classes. All that money."

"I know." Jyoti's voice wobbled. "I cried about it last night. Eighteen months. I really wanted it."

"So why not finish the course?"

"Because finishing it won't bring back the eighteen months. It'll just take six more."

"That's sad."

"It is sad. I'm letting it be sad. But I'm not ashamed. I learned how to learn a language. I made friends in class. That's not wasted."

"You sound very sure."

"I'm sure about tomorrow. Not about yesterday."

Aditi hugged her. "Okay. Sushi dinner to say goodbye to Japanese?"

"Deal. At least I can read the menu."

qa.q: How long had Jyoti been learning Japanese?
qa.a: A year and a half.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel about giving up Japanese?
qa.a: Jyoti felt sad and cried about the eighteen months, but was not ashamed.

qa.q: What question helped Jyoti decide, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Jyoti asked if she would start Japanese today, which focused on the future rather than the time and money already spent.

qa.q: How does Aditi seem to feel about Jyoti's decision?
qa.a: Aditi seems surprised at first but supportive, hugging Jyoti and suggesting a goodbye dinner.

grounding: A young woman asks if she would start a language course today, grieves the time spent and moves on without shame.

passage: Last March I sat in the lab in Aizawl with two years of fish samples in the freezer and a thesis going nowhere. My supervisor had moved to another university, the stream had changed course after the floods, and every new sample made the data messier. Lavanya, who shared my bench, found me staring at the freezer. "Go home, Lalremsiami," she said. I didn't. I asked myself the question an old teacher once gave me: if I were choosing a topic today, knowing all this, would I pick this one? I wanted to say yes. I couldn't. That night I cried properly, for the fieldwork, the muddy boots, the dawn buses. Then I wrote one page on what those years taught me: careful sampling, patience, asking for help sooner. In April I began a smaller project on the new stream bed. I'm not ashamed of that freezer anymore.

qa.q: What had happened to the stream?
qa.a: The stream had changed course after the floods.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami feel that night, and why?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt deep grief for the fieldwork, the muddy boots and the dawn buses, because the honest answer meant letting two years of work go 🤍

qa.q: Which step helped Lalremsiami move on without shame?
qa.a: Writing one page on what the two years taught, then starting a smaller project, so the lost time became learning instead of a reason to keep going.

qa.q: How might Lavanya be affected by Lalremsiami's decision?
qa.a: Lavanya is likely relieved to see Lalremsiami stop staring at the freezer and start fresh work that feels lighter.
